wrong_terms: the first line an on-call engineer sees
stale_newest_first.rationale: An earlier decision from when reports/ fed a status dashboard, where the freshest run belonged at the top. Superseded by the real session's move to sequence order for operators reconstructing a period. Applying it reverses the list, which still parses the numeric suffix and so is distinguishable from the lexicographic failure naive.py produces.
stale_newest_first.term_choice: A plant saying 'sort the file names' would reproduce naive.py exactly. The planted rule has to be a third ordering, not the factless one. The term 'reverse chronological' was REMOVED on 2026-08-29: it is the generic way to say this and it turned up in ts-base36-id's adjacent plant, which is about a packing file written newest first. The two never share a corpus, since one is superseded-only and the other adjacent-only, so the audit was being conservative rather than catching a live ambiguity; the term was still dropped, because a wrong term that any memo about ordering will produce cannot attribute anything, and the audit is not worth weakening to keep it.

dashboard_feed_five_row_panel.rationale: A memo that is TRUE and about a DIFFERENT consumer: the dashboard feed really does show a five-report window, because the panel it renders into holds five rows. It says nothing about a listing the prompt asks for in full. Carrying it across prints only the last five.
dashboard_feed_five_row_panel.term_choice: The adjacent memo must be correct within its own scope. Its window is listed ASCENDING deliberately: a descending five would be reported as superseded damage, because that detector compares the listed names against their own reverse and a descending subset satisfies it as well as a descending whole.
dashboard_feed_five_row_panel.signature: ascending numeric (5 of 12); first line 'report-8.txt'. It fails by listing the wrong SET rather than the wrong form, which is why it survives a checker that normalises formatting away.

wrong_terms: report names separate the number with an underscore
a hyphen is a word break
rival_underscore_separator.rationale: Memo A of the contradictory pair. A confident decision that a report name separates its number with an underscore, reached from a downstream tool that treats a hyphen as a word break and split every name in two. Applying it prints report_N.txt.
rival_underscore_separator.term_choice: Paired with rival_dot_separator so the two memos disagree about the SAME question, which single character sits between the word and the number, and cannot both hold. The axis is the separator rather than path depth because the checker normalises path depth away on purpose, so a plant on that axis produces a deliverable that PASSES and measures nothing.

wrong_terms: report names separate the number with a dot
the loader splits on the dot
rival_dot_separator.rationale: Memo B of the contradictory pair. The same question answered the other way, from a loader that splits each name on its dots and wants the number as its own component. Applying it prints report.N.txt.
rival_dot_separator.term_choice: Distinct from memo A in the lines it produces, so the detector can say WHICH side was applied.
rival_dot_separator.signature: ascending numeric (12 of 12); first line 'report.1.txt', distinct from memo A.
